nonObvious.text: The same softening cartridge lasts five months on one block and five weeks on another.
nonObvious.why: City water averages 1.8 grains of hardness per gallon, but reaches 7 where Croton water is blended in; the cartridge is rated in grains, not months.

nonObvious.text: A filter changed by the calendar is often already dead.
nonObvious.why: The spec sheet says replace when the rated volume is reached or once a year, whichever comes first; after the volume is used up it stops softening.

nonObvious.text: The warranty on a new espresso machine can be void from day one.
nonObvious.why: Dealers require installation by a certified technician and water treatment; scale and bad water are excluded.

nonObvious.text: A 240-volt machine in a 208-volt building is a quarter weaker.
nonObvious.why: Heating power falls with the square of the voltage; many commercial buildings supply 208 volts.

nonObvious.text: A dead compressor on a budget fridge means a new fridge.
nonObvious.why: The compressor job is quoted at $1,800-$2,800; the fridge costs $1,199.

nonObvious.text: Fridges die on the hottest day, when every technician is busy.
nonObvious.why: A dusty coil cannot shed heat in a hot room; service calls peak in June, July and August.

nonObvious.text: A six-hour blackout gets you nothing from Con Edison.
nonObvious.why: Spoilage claims start at more than 12 hours in 24 and only for failures of its own local system; the average network interruption is 6.7 hours, and food is lost after 2.

nonObvious.text: Storm outages are excluded from the utility claim.
nonObvious.why: Con Edison's tariff does not pay for conditions beyond its control; the state law steps in only after 72 hours.

nonObvious.text: You must tell the Health Department about your own power outage.
nonObvious.why: Health Code §81.43 requires immediate notice after a fire, flood or outage that may have left food out of temperature.

nonObvious.text: Taking cards offline moves the risk to you.
nonObvious.why: If a card is later declined, or the device is reset before it reconnects, the payment is gone and the seller is liable.

nonObvious.text: The busiest day is the worst day to break down.
nonObvious.why: Service is often next working day, Monday to Friday; weekend labor is billed at double.

nonObvious.text: A second grinder is cheaper than one day without espresso.
nonObvious.why: A day without espresso costs about 65% of $1,700 in sales; a second grinder is $2,099 and lasts six years.

nonObvious.text: The air conditioner on the roof is probably yours to replace.
nonObvious.why: Commercial leases usually make the tenant maintain and replace the unit that serves only its space; replacement runs $5,000-$12,000 plus a crane.

nonObvious.text: An ice machine nobody cleans is a health violation waiting for an inspector.
nonObvious.why: Ice is food; makers require cleaning about every 6 months; slime is cited as a dirty food-contact surface.

nonObvious.text: A fridge that drips into a bucket is a violation.
nonObvious.why: The inspection guide gives exactly that example under code 10B, improper drainage.

nonObvious.text: A missing $10 fridge thermometer is its own violation.
nonObvious.why: Code 10E: accurate thermometer not provided in refrigerated equipment, counted per unit.

nonObvious.text: The city knows whether you tested your backflow valve.
nonObvious.why: The annual report is filed with DEP, which mails a reminder and issues a summons when nothing arrives.

nonObvious.text: A handyman hookup can cost $6,000 even if you undo it.
nonObvious.why: Work without a permit: 21 times the permit fee, minimum $6,000, and removal does not avoid the penalty.

nonObvious.text: After a gas leak the building can be without gas for months.
nonObvious.why: The landlord repairs, the Buildings Department certifies, the utility tests; New York restaurants have waited two to seven months.

nonObvious.text: Roaches like the espresso machine best.
nonObvious.why: Warm, damp, full of crumbs; a technician finds them in about one machine in ten.

nonObvious.text: Coffee grounds are the cafe version of kitchen grease.
nonObvious.why: They pack the drain line with milk fat; plumbing is more than a quarter of restaurant repair calls.

nonObvious.text: Equipment is worth a fifth of its price the day you need to sell it.
nonObvious.why: Sellers get 10-30% of the original price; buyers at the same sale save 30-70%.

nonObvious.text: The free machine from the roaster is paid for in the price of beans.
nonObvious.why: The rent is built into the bean price and tied to a weekly minimum; below it the machine is not free.

nonObvious.text: Sales tax follows a lease payment by payment.
nonObvious.why: New York taxes each lease payment when it is paid.

nonObvious.text: Con Edison will pay most of the bill for efficient fridges and lights, but only if you ask first.
nonObvious.why: Up to 70% of the cost; work started before the offer letter does not qualify.

nonObvious.text: Buying equipment in December changes the tax bill for the whole year.
nonObvious.why: Section 179 lets the full cost be deducted in the year the equipment is placed in service.

nonObvious.text: In a heat wave the power does not just go out: it gets weaker.
nonObvious.why: Con Edison cuts voltage by 8% to protect cables; machines heat about 15% slower.

nonObvious.text: Old fridges are getting more expensive to repair every year.
nonObvious.why: The federal phasedown of older refrigerants is expected to raise their price 12-24% by 2029.

nonObvious.text: A scale on the counter needs a city seal.
nonObvious.why: Selling beans by weight makes the scale a commercial device: yearly inspection, $20.

nonObvious.text: Water main breaks are a winter event, and 2025 was the worst year in a decade.
nonObvious.why: 552 breaks in fiscal 2025, the most since 2015.

comparisons.text: Lending the espresso machine free of charge (comodato d'uso) against an exclusive coffee supply contract is the normal way a bar gets its machine; maintenance is included, and courts have enforced penalties for missing the minimum (one case: 144 kg a month).
Suppliers rent machines for a token sum against a minimum monthly coffee purchase, or for a fixed rent; service is not included by default and has to be negotiated.

Commercial espresso machines are pressure systems: the owner needs a written scheme of examination and a periodic boiler inspection certificate. No such requirement for cafe machines was found for New York City.
Equipment finance companies run programs where the roaster rents the machine and lends it to the cafe; the rent is built into the bean price, with tiers starting at 30 kg a week and 12-month terms.
